main.title: Ridge Racer V
main.summary: Ridge Racer V is a 2000 racing video game developed and published by Namco for the PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: Ridge Racer V
cards.text: Ridge Racer V is a 2000 racing video game developed and published by Namco for the PlayStation 2. It was released as a launch title for the console and later followed by an arcade version subtitled Arcade Battle. Ridge Racer V is the fifth main title of the Ridge Racer series following R4: Ridge Racer Type 4 and the only one to be released on PlayStation 2 (excluding the spin-off R: Racing Evolution).

cards.heading: Ridge City and a heavier soundtrack
cards.text: Ridge Racer V focuses on racing through the fictional Ridge City, with circuits built around the first course introduced in Ridge Racer. Its soundtrack also features a heavier sound, directed by Namco's Kohta Takahashi and featuring other Namco composers such as Nobuyoshi Sano and Yuu Miyake, as well as external contributions from Boom Boom Satellites and Mijk van Dijk. The game also introduced a new race queen mascot, Ai Fukami, replacing Reiko Nagase.

cards.heading: A PlayStation 2 launch under scrutiny
cards.text: Ridge Racer V accompanied PlayStation 2's original March 2000 launch. It received a positive reception for its visuals and speedy driving experience, but there was critique that it fell below expectations set by the console's promised graphics, and divided critics for some elements such as its lack of content compared to its predecessor and noticeable jaggies. However, in retrospect, it has been considered one of the greatest arcade-style racers of all time, with praise given to its handling, environments, and challenge.

main.title: Fantavision
main.summary: Fantavision, sometimes stylized as FantaVision, is a 2000 puzzle video game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: Fantavision
cards.text: Fantavision, sometimes stylized as FantaVision, is a 2000 puzzle video game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2. The game's objective is to use a cursor to select three or more launched fireworks (called "flares") of the same color in a row and then to detonate them to increase the player's score. Used in conjunction with various power-ups, the resulting explosions can ignite and chain together even more flares for additional points.

cards.heading: Fireworks as a PlayStation 2 showcase
cards.text: Fantavision was created during Sony's transition from its original PlayStation (PS1) to its next generation console. The game was initially conceived by director Katsuyuki Kanetaka, inspired by the fireworks shows he witnessed in his youth. After successfully pitching the project to Sony, Fantavision was supervised by the company's first-party development head Shuhei Yoshida and was completed by a small team in a short time frame. The graphics emphasize the PS2's ability to show particle effects.

cards.heading: Two-player additions and later releases
cards.text: Fantavision was released in Japan on March 9, 2000, a few days after the PS2 itself. It was released the same day as the console in North America, Europe, Australia, and New Zealand later that year with an added two-player mode. An updated version with this mode titled Futari no Fantavision was released in Japan in 2002, featuring revised cutscenes and design. Fantavision was then remade for Japanese mobile phones starting in 2003. Finally, the game was digitally re-released on Sony's newer consoles via the PlayStation Network outside of Japan beginning in 2015. The game received a mostly above-average critical response with reviewers generally praising its visual presentation, core gameplay, and multiplayer. However, many found fault with the length and replay value of its single-player experience when compared to contemporary titles in the puzzle genre.

main.title: Thief II: The Metal Age
main.subtitle: A thief in an industrial city
main.summary: Thief II: The Metal Age is Looking Glass Studios' first-person stealth adventure, released for Windows in March 2000. Garrett returns to a city where machinery and the religious Mechanists are gaining influence. Fifteen missions take him through guarded buildings and elaborate urban spaces. The objective is usually to steal, investigate or escape while remaining unnoticed. Darkness, footsteps and the surfaces underfoot matter as much as the route drawn on the map. A successful theft depends on understanding a place before acting inside it.

cards.heading: A thief in an industrial city
cards.text: Thief II: The Metal Age is Looking Glass Studios' first-person stealth adventure, released for Windows in March 2000. Garrett returns to a city where machinery and the religious Mechanists are gaining influence. Fifteen missions take him through guarded buildings and elaborate urban spaces. The objective is usually to steal, investigate or escape while remaining unnoticed. Darkness, footsteps and the surfaces underfoot matter as much as the route drawn on the map. A successful theft depends on understanding a place before acting inside it.

cards.heading: Reading the patrol
cards.text: Guards patrol rooms and corridors, reacting to sights and sounds. Garrett can observe their movements from cover, listen for approaching footsteps and wait for a passage to clear. A bright doorway may expose him even when the room beyond looks safe. Moving slowly across a noisy floor can be more useful than taking the shortest route. The levels allow several approaches, so an obstacle often invites another search through the building rather than a direct fight with its occupants.

cards.heading: Tools for another route
cards.text: Equipment changes what a route permits. Water arrows extinguish suitable flames, moss quietens surfaces and the blackjack can remove an unaware guard from a patrol. Rope arrows provide access where the material above can hold them. Supplies and mission conditions encourage deliberate choices: spending an arrow now may make the next crossing easier, while keeping it preserves another option. Thief II builds its tension around these preparations, letting a small adjustment to light, sound or access reshape a difficult room.

main.title: Metal Slug 3
main.subtitle: A campaign with more than one route
main.summary: Metal Slug 3 is SNK's run-and-gun adventure, first released for Neo Geo MVS in Japan on 23 March 2000.

cards.heading: A campaign with more than one route
cards.text: Metal Slug 3 is SNK's run-and-gun adventure, first released for Neo Geo MVS in Japan on 23 March 2000. The four-member squad returns to confront Morden's remaining forces and a renewed alien threat. Infantry shooting, rescued prisoners and powerful vehicles connect stages filled with extravagant creatures and machinery. Branching paths are its major addition, allowing a mission to lead through different hazards before rejoining at the boss. The choice gives repeated attempts another purpose: a familiar opening may now carry the player into a different stretch of the campaign.

cards.heading: Choosing the next battlefield
cards.text: Alternative routes can vary in length and difficulty, offering different equipment and opportunities to rescue prisoners. Choosing one therefore changes more than the scenery. A useful vehicle or weapon can affect how the next encounter is approached, while surviving preserves the score value of the people rescued along the way. Close attacks, grenades and found firearms remain the squad's basic tools. The branches make those familiar tools serve another sequence of problems, encouraging players to learn several ways through a mission rather than memorise a single uninterrupted path.

cards.heading: The scale keeps growing
cards.text: The campaign steadily increases the scale of its confrontations, moving from recognisable military enemies towards alien machinery and an extended final operation. Detailed animation keeps ordinary soldiers and small comic reactions visible inside the spectacle. The music includes work by Masato Horiuchi, Takushi Hiyamuta and Yoshihiko Wada. Metal Slug 3 draws its variety from the relationship between its simple controls and the situations built around them: another vehicle, transformation or route can change the immediate task while the player continues to run, jump and fire through the action.

main.title: Marvel vs. Capcom 2: New Age of Heroes
main.summary: Capcom and Marvel characters meet in a crossover fighting game built for the arcade. Its roster combines comic-book heroes with figures from Capcom’s game worlds.

cards.text: Marvel vs. Capcom 2: New Age of Heroes is a 2000 crossover fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It is the fourth installment in the Marvel vs. Capcom series, which features characters from both Capcom's video game franchises and comic book series published by Marvel Comics. The game received ports to the Dreamcast in 2000, the PlayStation 2 and Xbox in 2002, the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 in 2009, and iOS in 2012.

In Marvel vs. Capcom 2, players select a team of characters from the Marvel and Capcom universes to engage in combat and attempt to knock out their opponents. While the game uses similar tag team-based game mechanics to the series' previous iteration, Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (1998), it features several significant changes, such as three-on-three gameplay, a new character assist system, and a more simplified control scheme. The character artwork uses traditional 2D-animated sprites, while the backgrounds and visual effects are rendered in 3D. This makes Marvel vs. Capcom 2 the first game in the franchise to feature 2.5D graphics.

The game was acclaimed by critics, who praised its gameplay, visuals, and character roster, while criticizing its soundtrack, initial lack of online multiplayer support outside Japan, and game balance. Since its release, it has been considered one of the greatest games of all time especially in the fighting game genre. Following its release, Capcom lost the use of the Marvel Comics license, putting the series on a decade-long hiatus until the release of 2011's Marvel vs. Capcom 3: Fate of Two Worlds.

main.title: Colony Wars: Red Sun
main.subtitle: A civilian pilot chooses the next contract
main.summary: Colony Wars: Red Sun is Psygnosis' PlayStation space-combat game, first released in Europe on 24 March 2000. The third Colony Wars follows a miner who becomes a mercenary, moving away from the military allegiance that defined the earlier campaigns. Available contracts let the player choose which work to undertake before returning to the main story. Battles take place in space and within planetary atmospheres. The change in role gives each mission an additional practical purpose: successful work supplies the money needed to improve the ship that will carry out the next contract.

cards.heading: A civilian pilot chooses the next contract
cards.text: Colony Wars: Red Sun is Psygnosis' PlayStation space-combat game, first released in Europe on 24 March 2000. The third Colony Wars follows a miner who becomes a mercenary, moving away from the military allegiance that defined the earlier campaigns. Available contracts let the player choose which work to undertake before returning to the main story. Battles take place in space and within planetary atmospheres. The change in role gives each mission an additional practical purpose: successful work supplies the money needed to improve the ship that will carry out the next contract.

cards.heading: A better ship begins with the work it can complete
cards.text: Nine spacecraft offer different combinations of weapons and capabilities. Money earned by completing missions and destroying targets can purchase new craft or equipment, while predetermined slots limit how the chosen vessel can be configured. Interception and escort assignments ask for different priorities during combat. Large enemy ships also have individual components that can be targeted, making a turret a useful objective within a larger encounter. The player prepares for the job, then reads the battle for opportunities that suit the equipment brought into it rather than firing at every visible target indiscriminately.

cards.heading: The series opens its campaign to a mercenary career
cards.text: Only designated plot missions are required to advance the main story, leaving other contracts available as a way to earn resources and develop the ship. This structure gives Red Sun a more open rhythm than its predecessors without abandoning their cockpit combat. Gary McKill composed the score for the concluding PlayStation entry. Midway handled the delayed North American release later in 2000. Red Sun's distinctive contribution is the connection between choosing work and shaping a vessel: progress depends partly on deciding which available risk is worth taking before the next major story assignment.

main.title: Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards
main.subtitle: Two powers, a new possibility
main.summary: Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards brought HAL Laboratory’s pink hero to Nintendo 64, first releasing in Japan on March 24, 2000. Colourful polygonal scenery gives the series a new visual dimension while the main adventure follows side-scrolling routes. Kirby travels between planets to recover crystal shards, crossing grasslands, caves, deserts and seas. The contrast between rounded characters and varied environments preserves the series’ approachable personality while giving its familiar actions a new stage.

cards.heading: A crystal scattered across worlds
cards.text: Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards brought HAL Laboratory’s pink hero to Nintendo 64, first releasing in Japan on March 24, 2000. Colourful polygonal scenery gives the series a new visual dimension while the main adventure follows side-scrolling routes. Kirby travels between planets to recover crystal shards, crossing grasslands, caves, deserts and seas. The contrast between rounded characters and varied environments preserves the series’ approachable personality while giving its familiar actions a new stage.

cards.heading: Combining rather than replacing
cards.text: The defining idea is the combination of Copy Abilities. Kirby can use seven basic powers, then mix two to create a different attack instead of simply replacing one ability with another. Experimenting with combinations becomes part of exploring the stages and collecting the crystal shards. The main journey is a single-player adventure; a separate set of three minigames allows up to four players to compete.

main.title: MDK2
main.summary: MDK2 is a 2000 third-person shooter, action-adventure video game developed by BioWare and published by Interplay Entertainment for the Dreamcast, Windows and PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: One sequel, several platform versions
cards.text: MDK2 is a 2000 third-person shooter, action-adventure video game developed by BioWare and published by Interplay Entertainment for the Dreamcast, Windows and PlayStation 2. It is a sequel to the 1997 game MDK. First released for the Dreamcast in March 2000, it was later released for Windows in May, with newly selectable difficulty levels and the ability to manually save. In March 2001, a slightly reworked version, featuring level design modifications and gameplay tweaks, was released for the PlayStation 2 as MDK 2: Armageddon. The PC version was released on GOG.com in September 2008, and on Steam in September 2009. A port of the PlayStation 2 version was released for Wii via WiiWare in 2011. Also in 2011, a HD remastered version was released for Windows. Called MDK2 HD, this version features new 3D models, textures, improved lighting, and remastered music, and was released on Beamdog in October, and on Steam in July 2012.

cards.heading: Three characters change the style of play
cards.text: The game begins moments after the end of the original MDK. Believing they had vanquished the alien invaders, Kurt Hectic, Dr. Hawkins and Max are shocked to find a single Minecrawler remains. Kurt heads to destroy it, but upon doing so, encounters a massive alien called Shwang Shwing, who reveals the invasion of Earth is far from over. The main difference between MDK and MDK2 is the ability to control three playable characters (Kurt, Hawkins and Max), each with their own strengths and weaknesses. As such, the gameplay in the sequel is more varied than in the original game, with more emphasis on platforming and puzzles than straight run-and-gun shooting.

cards.heading: Variety praised, precision criticised
cards.text: MDK2 received generally positive reviews across all systems, with critics praising the graphics, variety of gameplay styles, level design, boss fights, the game's sense of humor, and its fidelity to the original MDK. The most commonly criticized aspects of the game were the difficulty level, which was felt to be too high, and the platforming sections, which many critics found frustrating and too exacting. Hawkins' levels in general were seen as inferior to Kurt's and Max's. In 2007, Interplay announced plans for a third game, but it was never made.

main.title: Power Stone 2
main.subtitle: A fight that falls out of the sky
main.summary: Four players compete for transforming stones while arenas collapse, move and carry the battle into new spaces.

cards.heading: Four fighters, one arena
cards.text: Power Stone 2 is Capcom’s arena fighting sequel, first released for the NAOMI arcade system in April 2000, with a Japanese Dreamcast edition arriving that month. Up to four players can fight together, collecting Power Stones and using objects scattered around the stage. Returning adventurers are joined by new characters, while the larger group makes every loose gem and weapon a contested prize. The action remains easy to read through running, jumping, grabbing and throwing, but an encounter can now be interrupted by two more fighters.

cards.heading: The stage moves too
cards.text: A stage can change while the match continues. On the aircraft, the fight begins aboard a plane that eventually breaks apart, sending the players into a free-falling battle before they reach another platform. Movement therefore responds to the place coming apart as well as to the other fighters. Weapons and supplies emerge from item boxes, adding another reason to cross the arena. Collecting three Power Stones still brings a transformation, allowing a player who has escaped the crowd to return with a brief advantage.

cards.heading: Items beyond the next match
cards.text: The Dreamcast Adventure mode gives collected objects a life beyond an individual match. Items and money go into an inventory, and the shop allows purchases or combinations that can produce something new. Unlocking more objects broadens what may appear in later battles, connecting the short encounters to a longer collection. A VMU application also lets players inspect and exchange inventory information. These additions sit beside the changing arenas: one part of the sequel builds a catalogue of toys, while the other repeatedly finds new places to use them.

main.title: MediEvil 2
main.subtitle: Sir Daniel wakes in the wrong century
main.summary: MediEvil 2 is Sony Cambridge's PlayStation action-adventure, first released in Europe on 21 April 2000. Sir Daniel Fortesque returns five hundred years after his earlier adventure, finding himself in Victorian London while Lord Palethorn's plans bring the dead back into the city. The change of period gives the familiar skeletal hero another kind of Gothic setting to stumble through. Weapons, exploration and eccentric encounters continue the original's mixture of horror and comedy. Daniel remains an unlikely champion, whose alarming appearance rarely matches the dignity with which he would like to be remembered.

cards.text: MediEvil 2 is Sony Cambridge's PlayStation action-adventure, first released in Europe on 21 April 2000. Sir Daniel Fortesque returns five hundred years after his earlier adventure, finding himself in Victorian London while Lord Palethorn's plans bring the dead back into the city. The change of period gives the familiar skeletal hero another kind of Gothic setting to stumble through. Weapons, exploration and eccentric encounters continue the original's mixture of horror and comedy. Daniel remains an unlikely champion, whose alarming appearance rarely matches the dignity with which he would like to be remembered.

cards.heading: A familiar hero in unfamiliar streets
cards.text: Dan can keep two weapons ready and switch between them during a fight. Pistols, blunderbusses and a gatling gun join his older swords and shields, while defeating enemies fills a Chalice of Souls that can earn further equipment. Later, placing his detached head on a zombified hand creates Dan Hand. The player can alternate between the crawling head and the body, exploring openings that the full skeleton cannot enter. The grotesque joke becomes a way to investigate the environment, giving an apparently familiar hero another useful shape.

cards.heading: A sequel made before the PlayStation moved on
cards.text: Sony commissioned the Cambridge team to continue MediEvil after the first game's favourable reception. Several concepts were considered before the Victorian Gothic revival became the chosen setting. James Shepherd directed, with Andrew Barnabas and Paul Arnold returning to compose the score. North America received the sequel in May 2000. Reviews generally welcomed the refinements while noting its close relationship to the original. MediEvil 2 keeps the series' personality intact by changing the place and period around Daniel, allowing a familiar comic figure to encounter another collection of wonderfully inappropriate dangers.
